newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jews of Hebron say Netanyahu misleading Israelis.
newsitem.headline: Jews of Hebron say Netanyahu misleading Israelis.

text.p: Jews in Hebron said on Wednesday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will have misled Israelis if he hands over 80 percent of the West Bank city to Palestinians as planned.
While Israeli and PLO negotiators struggled to sew up the long-delayed transfer, settlers spokesman Noam Arnon told reporters Jewish settlers feared a massacre by Palestinians.

Netanyahu, leader of the right-wing Likud party, ousted Labour leader Shimon Peres in May elections on a promise to better protect Israelis by getting tough with Israel's peace partner, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

"I don't know why and what might bring him -- I hope not -- to sign this agreement which very supposedly will cause the destruction of the community of Hebron," said Arnon, spokesman for the Hebron Jewish community, in English.
"If it is being signed and if he is going to implement the policies of the Labour government, I think he did not betray us but he misled the people," he said.

A statement issued by the umbrella council of the 130,000 Jewish settlers of the West Bank and Gaza said that based on their information, the Netanyahu-Arafat agreement was worse than that of the previous government.
Netanyahu wants to modify the Hebron deal with an eye to safeguarding the 532 Jews Arnon said live and study in the heart of the holy city surrounded by 120,000 Arabs.

Israel has completed many of the security arrangements for the transfer of the bulk of the city to Palestinian police. But all of the Jews and 15,000 to 20,000 Arabs will remain in the heart of the city under Israeli control, military sources say.

At Israeli military headquarters, a concrete building from British mandatory times due to be handed over to Palestinian rule, army spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Sharon Grinker said: "You can see the whole building is clean, painted and ready."
But Arnon said the Israeli army's security preparations underscored the settlers' feeling an accord with the PLO was anything but a peace deal.
"You can see how the army now is preparing itself for the new peace that is going to come -- how many walls and sandbags and bullet-proof positions," he said.

The volatile city, sacred to Moslem and Jew as the burial place of Abraham, is the last and most sensitive of seven West Bank Arab cities being handed over under a 1995 self-rule deal with the PLO and the only one with Jews living inside it.

"What we say today is that there is a potential massacre and pogrom again in Hebron," Arnon said, recalling the slaughter by Arabs in 1929 of some 60 Jews in Hebron. "We are surrounded by thousands of terrorists who want to kill us."
Palestinians in Hebron have the same fear of the Jews. U.S.-born Baruch Goldstein, a Jew from adjacent Kiryat Arba settlement, massacred 29 Palestinian worshippers in 1994.
An Israeli military source briefing reporters said tensions in the city were high, adding: "I see so many problems in Hebron, it's a very tough neighbourhood."

Arnon denied settlers were amassing arms beyond the firearms they are legally allowed to carry, despite a statement in parliament on Wednesday by Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani to the effect that such illegal weapons existed.

An opinion poll after Netanyahu's election showed a majority of Israelis favoured the Hebron deal but Arnon insisted that was not the case. As proof, he cited the roughly 60 percent of Israel's Jewish citizens who backed Netanyahu in the election.
But he acknowledged: "We are blamed for being here and we are blamed for how many soldiers have to protect us."
